ARC: The King for All (632–642)

=== EPISODE 1: Queen Sunduk (632)
A Queen? Ridiculous.
Munhee (26) is a young noblewoman, being attended by her low-rank servants. She is getting her hair done for an important event, while a servant takes care of her baby son Inmun (3).
munhee: Totally unfit for a Noble woman… Come on, boy, can’t you find something better?
Her husband Chunchu is dressing too. He is twenty-nine, and already the most cunning man in Samhan. Only the quiet rooms know it yet. Their two children are getting under everyone's feet.
Bupmin is six. He finds his father and uncle on the hill where adults invent countries and sits down without being asked.
munmu: When I’m king everyone has to listen to me. / Even the bone people. / …And the ones with no bone. Those most, there’s more of them.
munhee: Listen to him. / He gets the sentences from you. The volume is his own.
chunchu: …Keep that. / I may need to borrow it back when I am braver.
Before they dress for the hall he takes the two of them around the palace road. Gotaso sits in front of him on the same horse. Bupmin has his own, and will not share the saddle.
gotaso: Faster. / Father. Faster.
chunchu: You'll bite your tongue. / Then you'll talk less, which — wait, that's the joke? Fine. Hold on.
munmu: I'm not racing. / I'm following. That's different.
chunchu: That's a lawyer's horse, son. / Look at you. I'm going to tell your mother you invented a new kind of slow.
King Jinpyung (65) is dead, after years of expanding Silla against Baekje.
Silla runs on bone. Your rank is your birth, and your birth is your life. Six common ranks at the bottom. Above them, the nobles. Above them, the royals.
[diagram bone-rank]
In the hall the sleeves are the census. True Bone wears purple 자색. Head Rank Six wears scarlet 비색. Five wears blue 청색. Four and below wear yellow 황색. You can read a man before he speaks.
alchun: Below all of them are the slaves — but those are not counted as people.
sunduk: …A country that does not count people as people. How is that meant to last a thousand years?
Three royals are left. All three are the old king's daughters. Dukman, thirty-seven. Seungman, thirty-two. Chunmyung, fifty-two. That is the whole bloodline, and all of it is women.
Which of the three it will be is settled the night before, in a pavilion off the pond, by six men and a brazier. By morning the palace has a name, and the name has to be dressed.
sunduk: I put on this confident face, / but honestly — me, becoming king… / I wonder whether I can do it at all…
yushin: Whether you do it well or badly — / that is what “no matter what” means. / In all this world, wouldn’t it be good to have one person always on your side, Princess? / Hwarang Kim Yushin. / I will serve you to the end.
And so she becomes the first Queen of Silla. They will call her Queen Sunduk, the Blue Moon of the Divine Country.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Royal Chronology (王曆) — Queen Seondeok] The sacred-bone males were exhausted, and therefore a queen was set up.
Munhee's big brother is Yushin. He is thirty-seven, and he runs the yard. Horse, bow, gyuku: that is where boys learn whether they matter. People call him the Sword of Silla. He is also, everyone notices, very fond of the princess.
The capital’s daughters follow the Sword of Silla around the yard. He does not look at them. He looks only at the Queen.
courtmaid: The marshal walked past. / I know. Don’t look. / …I’m looking.
courtmaid: The most popular man in Silla, and he will not even turn his head. / If he smiled once the colonnade would fall over.
Then the yard-coat is open down the spine, and She sees the width of his back — muscle the court is not supposed to want — and the Queen’s face goes vermilion before she can pretend it is the lamp.
He and Chunchu had known each other since they were boys. There is a story about that, though neither of them tells it the same way twice.
[FLASHBACK 612 the east star]
  Two boys on a hill above Surabol, lying on their backs, arguing about the sky.
  chunchu: Brother. That star, in the east. / That one’s the brightest, isn’t it?
  yushin: That is a planet, not a star, you idiot.
  chunchu: Even better. It sits among the stars without being one of them. / Just like you.
  yushin: ……
  chunchu: Brother. Let us make Samhan one country. / No Goguryeo, no Baekje, no Silla. Just… people. / And over them, one king for all of them.
  yushin: “A king for all.” / …You be that. I will stand beside you.
  chunchu: That is a promise, then.
yushin: Are you feeling alright, your majesty?
sunduk: Hm? (startled)
yushin: Look at me. / Not the door. (smiles)
For a moment neither of them says anything. Then she straightens, and she is the Queen again.
yushin: …Once.
sunduk: Once what.
yushin: Call me by name, not by title. / Today, since it is the last day for it.
sunduk: …Yushin-ah.
Nobody in the room hears it. It is the last time in forty-one years that anyone calls him that, and he will still be able to hear it on the day he dies.
sunduk: Lord Yushin. / My sister married for love and got a son out of it. / I got a council that sat until dawn.
yushin: …Your Majesty.
sunduk: So from now on — «Your Majesty». Nothing else. / …That is what I have.
Then the young knights kneel and pledge themselves to the throne. Bidam kneels in front, already the yard's Second Blade. Pumsuk is fourteen, and trying very hard not to look it.
hwarang: By Hyukgosé’s light, we, the young Hwarang knights of Silla, pledge eternal allegiance to the Queen!
At the end of the ceremony, everyone chants for their new queen.
May the heavenly White Horse bless this queen… Long live the Queen! Long live the Hwarang spirit! Long live Silla!
?: (market woman, to a child) / Remember where you live. The Divine Country. The Rooster Forest. / Kings change. Get the name right.
Blue banners. A moon no one has to point at. In the capital they have already raised a tower to read the stars — Cheomseongdae.
Silla sends envoys to the other kingdoms to let them know of their new queen.
kingmu: So that old brat Jinpyung is finally dead… Bah! Good riddance. And they have seated a daughter, eh…?
yeongnyu: Let us see how long that Council of theirs lasts.
taizong: A woman king… those Samhan barbarians are at it again, aren’t they? Wu! Prepare my robes.
He sends her a gift: a painting of peonies in three colours, and a packet of their seeds.
sunduk: …There are no butterflies on these flowers.
alchun: Your Majesty?
sunduk: It means no scent. / …And the Second Emperor would like me to know he has noticed I have no husband.
She has the seeds planted anyway. When they bloom, they have no scent. The court decides she is a sage. She knows she simply reads people.
jomei: First my aunt, and now Silla as well…? It must be a new trend.
Sun, for kindness.
Duk, for virtue.
Six men who hate the word “woman” crowned one anyway. How? Go back one night, to a brazier…!

=== EPISODE 2: Harmony Council (632)
## The Night Before
The Harmony Council meets to debate who the next king should be. Six nobles, one night. Nobody stands up until they all agree.
Night in a small pavilion off the pond. Someone lights the small brazier. The flame is red first.
It runs hotter. The flame turns blue. Only then may the session start.
Each sleeve has a cup of tea and a wooden piece on a personal mat. They vote by setting the piece on either side of the cup.
The Council decides by unanimity. One voice against is enough to stop a name. That is why it takes all night, and why the room fears the newest member almost as much as it fears a woman on the throne.
The first count is three to three. A hung jury in silk. Initial vote, then deliberation, then a final vote that cannot move until every sleeve agrees.
Three pieces go to the yes side of the cup. Three go to the no side.
[diagram harmony-council]
alchun: The first count is split. / Half this room still says a woman cannot rule.
How about Prince Chunchu…? Chunchu’s mother is a Royal, but his father is a Noble… In that case, the child becomes a Noble as well.
[FLASHBACK 612 The night bridge · 귀교]
  Chunchu is nine. His father wakes him past midnight, which is normal, and walks him to the stream below the palace, which isn't. Kim Yongsu is the son of a king the Council threw out. The capital has a word for him that it only says after he leaves. He talks to the dark. He laughs a beat late. He adds a granary ledger faster than the clerk can read it.
  Tonight he is laying flat stones across the water by lamplight, one at a time, as if someone on the far bank were waiting for the bridge to be finished before dawn.
  yongsu: Shh. They’re working. / …No, don’t look for them. They hate being looked at. Like me.
  chunchu: Father… who is?
  yongsu: Your grandfather sat in the big chair four years. Three counts, and the room took it back. / That room eats the men who amuse it. / So— stay out of that room. Sit anywhere else. Sit on the bridge.
  chunchu: …If not in the room, where does a person sit?
  yongsu: (laughs, a beat late) / Wherever the room has to come to you.
  By morning there is a bridge of flat stones across the stream that nobody in the palace remembers ordering. The servants say goblins. Chunchu, who carried the lamp, says nothing at all, and finds he is good at it.
How about the Kim of Gaya…? The Marshal’s blood is royal — in a country that no longer exists. Yes, and if we begin counting kingdoms that no longer exist, half this room is royal.
The Royal blood, there remain only three… The woman king, finally we shall see…
The newest member of the Council — a Hwarang barely seated among them — stands up.
bidam: My lords have said one word forty times tonight. “Woman.” / I have known Princess Dukman since I was a boy. / Not one of you has ever put a question to her that she could not answer. / If only three of the Sacred Bone remain, then I choose the cleverest of the three.
murim: …If cleverness picks a king, whose cleverness do we hear tomorrow. / Bone is the measure. Bone does not change.
imjong: The bone has run out. / Holding a country on empty bone is more dangerous than a clever woman.
suljong: I still… cannot raise my hand. / This room is too old to be turned by one night’s speech.
yushin: I have put questions to her. / They were answered. Half this room never asked — they only repeated the word woman. / That is what deliberation is for. To overturn the first count.
yumjang: …Alchun. Only your hand is left.
alchun: I have taken a tiger. / A tiger has no sex. It has teeth. / …I raise it. Final vote.
Alchun moves his piece. All six sit on the yes side.
[diagram harmony-council]
alchun: …That boy Bidam has no fear in him at all.
Across the floor, Yushin catches the Second Blade's eye. He and Bidam have been trading wins since they were boys in the yard. The count stands at one hundred and eight apiece. Neither lets the other stay ahead for long.
yushin: Well stood. / Tomorrow on the yard — the hundred-and-ninth is mine.
bidam: Come now, brother. / Today is the country’s business. The blade can wait till tomorrow.
High Councillor
They argue past midnight. In the end there is nothing left to argue with — the blood runs out before the objections do, and Dukman is queen.
Every sleeve in that room learned to fight in one dead king’s yard. Who was he? Back we go, to the Cloud King…!

=== EPISODE 3: Jinheung, the Cloud (554) [flashback]
Ask anyone in Surabol about the Cloud King and they'll tell you about his stones. Ask anyone in Sabi and they'll change the subject. You'll find out why. Not yet.
He was seven when they put the crown on him. It was too big, and nobody mentioned it. By the end, Silla had a river, a coastline and Gaya. He got there by being the best ally in Samhan, right up until the afternoon he wasn't.
He put up stones wherever he stopped — four of them, on mountains, at the edges of what he had taken — and the stones do not boast. They say who came, and when, and that the land is now inside the border. They are property deeds.
herald: There is no boasting on this stone at all.
herald: Boasting is for men who are worried about losing it.
Late in his reign he invents the Hwarang. Take the noblest boys and put them in one yard. Make them ride, sing and rank each other until the ranking feels like fate. Nearly every man who matters later comes out of that yard.
One class a year. The number sticks to a man for life. Almost every sleeve on the Council first slept in that hall.
[diagram hwarang]
Chunchu. Yushin. Bidam. Pumsuk. Alchun. Gwanchang. Wonsul. They are all, in the end, one old man’s idea about what to do with teenage boys.
Near the end he shaved his head. The king of the four mountain stones put on a monk's robe and took a new name: Dharma Cloud. His queen went into a nunnery beside him. The court kept calling him Majesty. He kept answering to the other thing.
Long after the stones are mossed over, the old men of the capital still argue about what to call him. Not in the official registers — those keep to temple names — but in the quiet after the wine.
elder: Jinheung… we called him the Cloud King. After the name he took at the end. / A cloud has no border, you see. It goes where it likes, and for an afternoon the ground underneath is its ground.
herald: That sounds like praise.
elder: It was, for about a year. / Then you look at where the shade fell. Gwansan. The Han. Gaya. / A cloud never asks whose field it’s raining on.
That rain fell on Baekje’s field. Baekje kept the grudge. Now meet the prince who will inherit it…!

=== EPISODE 4: Prince Euija (632)
Thirty-two is late to be named crown prince. By the time his father gets around to it, Euija has more than fifteen sons. The clans have had years to decide which ones they own.
In Sabi the clans read the stars the way other courts read ledgers. Loyalty is the word they use when the door between king and house is still closed; after it opens, they use other words.
herald: …Fifteen?
herald: His Majesty has over fifty — Samsin must keep a night shift just for Sabi. The Crown Prince is still comfortably behind.
This is said admiringly. It is that kind of court.
The young princes grow up already spoken for. Yung is the eldest. Pung is eight and has good handwriting. Each boy wears a clan's ring, hears a clan's tutor, and finds a clan's grudge folded into his allowance.
kingmu: Crown Prince. / There. Now they have to bow to you first and complain about you second.
euija: They complained first for thirty-two years, Father. / I’ll take the bow.
Prince Euija (32)
Euija sneaks out of the palace to explore the life of the common people.
The boy is going back into the water. He has been at it since morning, and he is not a strong swimmer.
euija: How many times have you gone in?
gyebek: Nineteen.
euija: …You were counting?
gyebek: At twenty I would not come back out. That is why I count.
euija: Are you insane?! In that much of a hurry to stand before Yumla?!
gyebek: I gave my word.
It takes a while to get it out of him.
[FLASHBACK  No name]
  The houses go first. Silk burns faster than timber. He is still wearing the clothes they dressed him in for the morning meal.
  They tell him to run and not say the name. He says it once, into his sleeve, and then he does not.
  After that he begs. The noble collar is dirty enough that nobody bows.
euija: A fine young man… what is your name?
gyebek: I have… no name.
euija: …What? You think it makes sense to have no name, here in Baekje?
euija: It’s the name of a great man. / How about — “Gyebek”?
It is the White River — the wide mouth below Sabi where clan barges quarrel over winter space, and where boys who cannot swim keep trying anyway.
gyebek: …Do you like the name, or do you like me?
euija: …People don’t usually ask that.
gyebek: I have to ask, or I do not know.
Prince Yung is the favored one to win — oldest, strongest, and backed the way favorites are always backed: by houses that have already counted what he will owe them. In the succession the clans are not watching. They are holding the brackets.
Eight houses. Eight fighting styles. One king between them. And every house has already picked a prince…!

=== EPISODE 5: Eight Great Clans (632)
Satek. Yunbi. Jinmo. Mokli. Hae. Baek. Guk. Ahn.
The Eight Great Clans run this country, and one king sits between them. Satek fights with the king's sleeve. Yunbi fights with the coast road. The other six keep their techniques quiet.
Once a year, the court chalks a square grid in the palace yard. Four hard lines. No banners. The young men of each house step onto the grid in white. It's the same quarrel as the west bridge, only without the carts.
eldersatek: White cloth. Wooden swords. / If anyone bleeds the wrong colour, the berth talks stop for a month.
elderyunbi: Then keep your boys’ wrists honest. / The chalk does not care whose sleeve they hold.
Swords first. Wooden ones, which still remember steel. A Jinmo boy holds his blade high. A Satek boy answers from the middle. On the call they both move. Blades skim the chalk. The white sleeves clap together so close that the steps gasp.
🗣: That Jinmo boy? / Short wrists. / Feet faster than the Satek though. / Point to the white sleeve.
When the wooden points are tallied, the sand comes out. A circle of grit inside the same square. Ssireum — satba locked before they stand, knees in the grit, equal grips on waist and thigh, then up without letting go. No circling for a hold. The bout is the hold.
A Hae boy hooks a leg. A Guk boy answers with his hip. He lifts, he turns, and the other boy's feet leave the earth. The yard goes quiet the way a dock goes quiet when a rope snaps. Sand takes the shoulder. The chalk does not argue.
eldersatek: See? / Even Yunbi can fall without a cart.
elderyunbi: Your boy’s knee touched first. / Ask the chalk. / Elders watch from the hall steps — they always do — and still count wrong when it is their sleeve.
By dusk the white is grey with chalk and grit. Nobody has settled four generations of anything. The throne likes it that way. The boys go home with a score instead of a funeral.
The Satek clan is currently the most powerful. Both the Queen and the Premier are from the Satek clan, making them a key rival to the royal Buyeo clan.
Elder Satek
Minister Satek
Queen Satek
Satek Chunbok
In the Assembly they fight for power, each house holding a share of the king's sons. They fight in the street too. Same fight. The street version is older.
[diagram eight-clans]
[diagram ministers-assembly]
Unlike Silla’s Harmony Council, the Assembly does not require every voice. A plurality of houses is enough — which is why the street fights matter. Votes can be bought in pieces. In Surabol they must be bought entire, or not at all.
What the Assembly votes on, more often than war, is water. Who loads first. Whose ships winter in the river mouth. Who gets the orange levy, and who gets the silk berth. In this country, a clan without a harbour can't feed a fight.
eldersatek: Yunbi talks of blood. / We talk of berths. / Blood cools. A winter anchorage does not.
elderyunbi: You hold the king’s sleeve and call it a harbour. / We hold the coast road. Sabi to the salt. Every cart that fears rain pays us in quiet.
Satek and Yunbi have been at it for four generations. Nobody alive can say what started it. Everybody alive can list the last six things.
🗣: The Yunbi boys turned a Satek cart over at the west bridge yesterday. / Then tonight the Satek go over a Yunbi wall. / Same as the lantern festival last year. / Last year three of them died.
eldersatek: Yunbi is not Baekje blood. They rolled in from the north.
elderyunbi: We rolled in four hundred years ago. / Does that not make us Baekje by now?
eldersatek: Four hundred years rolling in. Four hundred rolling out.
elderyunbi: Satek is a house that lives by holding the king’s sleeve. / We do not hold the sleeve. We hold the arm.
Neither house has ever won, and nothing about that is accidental: the throne needs both of them standing. A clan with no rival starts watching the throne.
The rivalry has a quieter register, too — the kind that never makes the street. Each house keeps a clerk in the other’s counting-room. Each house denies it. Every third Assembly, someone finds a cup under a floorboard that was not there when the session opened, and both sides pretend to be shocked.
🗣: They say Yunbi already knows what was said in the Satek meeting. / And Satek already knows the Yunbi one. / So both know, and both pretend not to. / That’s politics.
Once, both houses secretly agreed to kill a grain levy. It came to the Assembly anyway. The votes lined up as counted. Then Elder Satek, who had nodded all morning, turned his thumb down at the last call. The levy died. Yunbi's men stared. His own men stared harder. He never explained.
👑 King Mu (71)
kingmu: Lord Yunbi… an honour to— / Lord Satek… a new—
euija: Father… I have no interest in these clan quarrels. / A king should be for the country—
kingmu: My child… learn their names anyway. / …I did not like mine either. I still say them first.
“Restore the reign of the thirteenth Eraha!” Every house in Sabi still chants it. To hear why, we go back three hundred years…!

=== EPISODE 6: Gunchogo, the 13th (371) [flashback]
Baekje’s thirteenth king marches north to Pyongyang. A Goguryeo king dies on his own wall. In seven hundred years, it never happens again.
Baekje has the river, the coast and the sea roads east. The clans take the docks. The throne takes a cut. It is the richest kingdom in Samhan, and the strongest. Neither lasts.
nation-baekje: Restore the reign of the thirteenth Eraha.
They will still be chanting that sentence three centuries later, in a courtyard, to a clever king who has already decided that a country is a story. It is the sentence that gets Daeya burned.
Goguryeo remembers it too, and differently, and for exactly as long.
Back to the snow, and to Goguryeo’s most frightening commander. First question: do you know what happens to traitors…?

=== EPISODE 7: Commander Yeon (634)
In the high mountains of Manchuria, a young man is caught in the snow by a Goguryeo soldier.
He is taken to the outpost of Commander Yeon (29), the Eternal General — a ruthless military general.
gesomun: Do you know what happens to traitors, young man...?
It is over quickly, and it is not clean. Nobody in the yard looks away, because looking away is also a report.
The guards talk about him the way men talk about weather. “He’s a monster, you know. Out here they call him the Red Sun of Pyongyang. He’s made the Eastern Commandery the safest in the kingdom. The barbarians run if they hear his name.”
The outpost is also a building site. Three summers ago, the Tang flattened Goguryeo's pile of enemy bones. Goguryeo got the message. Now it builds a wall. A thousand li of it. When Yeon isn't killing anybody, he walks it with a plumb line and kicks the crooked stones.
gesomun: They say you… leaked our secrets to the enemy. / Do you know what punishment is given to a traitor?
Prisoner: I have… no name.
gesomun: Of course. The barbarians always show more respect.
A month before the Summit, in a Mohe village the Eastern Command has finished with, there is a boy who will not move out of the doorway of a house that no longer has a roof. Snow is settling on the ash. He has a shaved crown and two braids, and he holds a stick the way he has seen men hold spears. Yeon gets down off the red bay and walks up until the stick touches his chest.
gesomun: Move.
gulgul: …
gesomun: Do you understand me.
gulgul: …
He does not. Yeon looks at him for what his officers later agree was an unreasonable length of time. Then he laughs, the slap of a laugh they will learn to dread, and pulls off his gloves.
gesomun: Look at this one. Guarding a house that’s already burned. / Good. This is what Goguryeo looks like. / Get on. The second horse.
He hands the gloves down. They do not fit. The boy gets on the second horse anyway, the stick still in his fist.
dosuryu: …You are taking him?
gesomun: Where do you think that boy is standing when he is grown.
dosuryu: …Opposite us, I should think.
gesomun: That is why I am taking him.
He gives him the name Gulgul, which is not a Goguryeo name and is not a Mohe one either, and raises him in Pyongyang alongside his own sons — one step behind them at every meal.
Years later, on the north wall of Pyongyang in a winter worse than this one, Yeon stands with the grown boy a step behind him and the river frozen white below. He says the thing he says every winter, to anyone in earshot, as if the cold might forget it otherwise.
gesomun: Cold?
gulgul: …No, sir.
gesomun: Liar. I’m cold too. / Remember it anyway. Kings die, courts get tired, walls come down— / Goguryeo never dies.
Gulgul grows up quiet. When Yeon sends him to guard the northern marches, he gives him a surname. Dae. Big, as big as the country. Dae Gulgul watches that border for thirty years, and nobody writes down anything else about him. They write a great deal about his son.
The summons isn't addressed to him. It's addressed to his father, who still holds the Eastern seal. Yeon Taejo sat in the capital's big chair for twelve years. Now he is too old to ride that far. The son has done the work for years. The seal is still the old man's.
yeontaejo: Take the seal. You sit in my place this year. / …And say half of what you think.
gesomun: Me? Why do I have to go to Pyongyang? / It’s a place where mouths open only to say useless things…
yeontaejo: I know. I sat in it for twelve years. / Half, son. Half.
He promised his father half. He has never said half of anything. Next stop: Pyongyang, and a room full of men counting grain…!

=== EPISODE 8: High Summit (634)
So Yeon rides to Pyongyang in his father's place. Five commanders, one king, one room. They call it the High Summit.
He rides in at the red two-tier gate. Pyongyang already knows the sound of those hooves.
Goguryeo works like this. Five commanders argue. The High Commander holds the first sword. The king has the last word.
[diagram high-summit]
The chamber is already loud when Yeon arrives — not with strategy, with arithmetic. Every banner wants a larger share of the same winter grain.
yeongnyu: Enough. / I did not call five commands to Pyongyang to divide a granary. / I will be the “King for All” — Samhan under one roof. Silla and Baekje first.
southcmd: Then the Southern Command takes the next levy. / Yushin’s banners have been testing the passes. If His Majesty wants Samhan, give me men — not speeches.
northcmd: And leave the north bare? / The Mohe burned three villages last frost — Haemosu’s sun does not reach the north in winter, and neither do Central’s warehouses. I need the cavalry remounts promised at the last Summit.
westcmd: The Liao watch needs timber and iron, not another southern adventure. / If we strip the west to chase Samhan, we gift the Tang a road.
gusesa: (mild, as if chairing a feast) / Each front believes it is the only front. That is why we meet. / Eastern Command has kept the marches quiet. Let us not reward noise over results.
westcmd: My grandfather still toasts Ulchi at the Colossal River — Salsu, the old men say — as if a drowned Sui host were a harvest. / Ansi’s walls are not a toast. They are a bill we keep paying in stone.
gesomun: Then stop paying the West in gold for another quiet decade. / Rivers remember who feeds them. So do fortresses.
gesomun: Quiet? / I have been killing tribes so this room can argue about who gets the horses. / Meanwhile the Second Emperor — Li Shimin — is not a tribute account. He is a man who murders brothers for a throne and then invents a reason.
yeongnyu: Commander Yeon. Watch your tongue about foreign kings. / We have bought decades with gold. We will buy more — and spend the peace on Samhan.
gesomun: You cannot buy a man who has already decided the price of your head. / I have watched how courts die: they starve the wall that is screaming, and fatten the wall that flatters. / Give the west grain. Give the north horses. Give the south whatever fairy tale you like — / but do not sit here pretending the Second Emperor is a weather we can ignore because tribute is habit.
southcmd: Easy for the East to lecture. You fight people without cities. / I fight Kim Yushin. Send me the next levy or stop talking about Samhan.
northcmd: And I will not freeze another winter while Central counts my remounts twice.
westcmd: Nor will I strip the Liao for a king’s poem about one peninsula.
Yeon’s hands are flat on the table. The nails have gone white. This is the face of a man who has already fought the war the room refuses to schedule.
gesomun: Listen to yourselves. / Horses. Timber. Bodies. A crown-word. / When the Second Emperor comes he will not ask which of you was most polite in committee.
gusesa: If you keep defying the king, Commander Yeon… / we may have to name you a traitor.
gusesa: (to Yeon, almost kindly — which is worse) / Nephew. Sit down. The Summit does not run on prophecies.
gesomun: …. / Then keep your Summit. / Keep your tribute. Keep your Samhan dream carved into a budget fight. / When the Second Emperor’s drums reach the Liao, remember who tried to spoil the feast.
He walks out before it ends. Outside, the corridor is very long and very cold. Behind him the chamber returns to numbers — as if he had never brought an emperor into the room.
gesomun: Heaven above… help this foolish country…!
In the yard the Eastern banners answer him anyway — a roar that has nothing to do with the Summit’s minutes.
dosuryu: Look at that — see how Pyongyang loves you.
gesomun: Of course. The people have never once abandoned me. / It is the politicians…!
gesomun: His Majesty wants Samhan under one roof. / The Summit wants the roof itemised. / …Get the horses. I would rather sleep in a tent tonight.
## Birth of Namseng
Yeon’s wife labours in a Goguryeo timber chamber blasted white with daylight — no extra bodies, no portrait-frame crowd. Only the midwife who opens a birth, and the mother. The rest of the world falls out of the light.
yeonwife: Samsin… / This child alone — please. / …This time — please.
The portrait does not stay paint. Samsin steps from the frame the way steam steps from a kettle — one midwife of the living world under Little Star — and lays a hand where mortal hands have failed.
samsin: Do not weep. / I will open the breath. / The name — that is yours to give.
So the first heir arrives under Samsin's hand, the year of the Summit. They call him Namseng. A son is born. Nobody wanted a poem in the name. It's the sound the room makes when the baby breathes.
gesomun: Namseng. / …Heavier than it sounds. / This country. You will have to keep it.
Once, Goguryeo did not argue about grain. It had a king with sixty-four fortresses. To meet him, we go back two centuries…!

=== EPISODE 9: Gwanggaeto, the Great King (400) [flashback]
Silla is drowning. An army from across the sea is inside its walls. Then Gwanggaeto sends fifty thousand horsemen south, and the Wa are gone.
A red sun. The three-legged crow rides south on his banners. The stele will list sixty-four fortresses. It will not list the nerve it took.
Sixty-four fortresses, one reign. The stele at his tomb lists them all.
Silla had asked. That's the part everyone forgets. A Silla king, with foreigners inside his capital, sent north and begged. Fifty thousand horsemen came down and cleared the peninsula. Then they didn't leave for fifty years.
herald: They did save us.
herald: So why are they still here?
Silla’s crown princes go north as hostages. Silla’s court takes Goguryeo titles. Silla’s army takes Goguryeo orders. It lasts two generations. Silla does not forget it.
Two hundred and forty years later a Silla prince will stand in front of a foreign emperor and ask for an army, and every single person in Surabol will know exactly what that costs, because it has been done to them before.
[QUOTE Gwanggaeto Stele (廣開土王碑), south face, ll. 3–4 (414 CE); Best, “The Kwanggaeto Stele,” p. 147] The common people were at peace in their work; the country was rich and the people abundant; the five grains ripened in plenty.
Bupmin is fifteen now. The Hwarang have five rules, and his uncle has one question: which will you break first…?
